items.title: FlowTranslator: Training-Free In-Image Machine Translation with Flow-Based Editing
items.text: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. items.text: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. items.text: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. items.text:
Codex this week: 9 changes, 5 user pain points, all here.



Oct 25 to Nov 1, checked against OpenAI's posts, help pages and GitHub.



Releases

1. GPT-6.1 Terra rolled out in Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu (Oct 26). Tibo says it gives 2x the usage of 6.1 Sol.

2. CLI v0.165.0 (Oct 27): built-in Vertex AI provider, change reasoning effort mid-chat, memory v2 on by default.

3. CLI v0.166.0 (Oct 29): Terra in the Vertex AI and Bedrock catalogs, codex doctor --network-only, transcript search, and a fix for early compaction after resume or fork.

4. Text your dot over iMessage or RCS (Pro, US preview). Multi-account switching landed on mobile, with desktop "coming soon".



Limits and pricing

5. Limits doubled for Pro 100, 200, 500 and Business Premium, and the Oct 30 Pro 200 cut was cancelled.

6. Pro and Business now get monthly API credits ($100 to $500 on Pro). They don't raise your Codex allowance.

7. Confirmed: from December, ChatGPT and Codex share one token-based allowance on Plus, Pro and Business.

8. New device limits: one machine can only hold so many paid accounts, or you get "Device limit reached".

9. Banked reset 1 of 2 is live. Redeem it in Usage settings or with /usage in the CLI.



Incidents and security

- Oct 27: GPT-6.1 Sol was degraded for about 78 minutes, then resolved.

- Don't run Codex inside ~/Downloads (Forever Security found a planted AGENTS.md), and don't install it from reseller one-liners (Symantec caught one turning the sandbox off).

- Forever Security says a local HTML page opened in Codex's built-in browser can read files on disk. Still unpatched as of Oct 29, per their write-up.



What users are saying

- 429 and "at capacity" errors with most of the allowance left, mostly VS Code on Linux. The busiest new GitHub issue this week (#57084, 87 comments). No fix yet. Switch models with /model, and codex resume picks the session back up.

- VS Code extension 26.1021.22027 "could not start its user interface" on Linux and Windows, across several issues. Reported workarounds: the pre-release build, an older version, or launching with code --disable-gpu.

- Usage rings vanished from the desktop app sidebar after recent updates (#57656, Windows and Mac). Check Settings > Usage or /status meanwhile.

- Max or Ultra missing from the reasoning slider after 26.1027 (#58201). Fix confirmed by several users: Settings > General > Available reasoning efforts, re-check the level.

- The shared December pool is the loudest topic on X, and a GitHub request to keep Plus allowances separate is gaining votes (#58530).



What people are asking OpenAI for: publish how chat and Codex tokens will be counted before December, bring the usage rings back, post a status note when 429s hit accounts with quota left, and give a fix date for the built-in browser issue.



Community shoutout

@talkaboutdesign built agent-stat, which shows your local Codex usage, per-request cost and live limits in one place: npx agent-stat@latest



Tip

Hold your banked reset until you need it. It only redeems once an allowance is under 80% remaining, and it moves your weekly reset date to the day you use it.



Sources: openai/codex releases and issues on GitHub, help.openai.com, @thsottiaux and @OpenAI on X

items.title: EEFA: A Framework for the Ethical Evaluation of AI Agents
items.text: The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents across consequential domains including healthcare, legal services, nancial management, and enterprise workows has created an urgent governance challenge. While the eld of AI evaluation has produced sophisticated benchmarks for measuring agent capability, these frameworks measure exclusively what agents can do rather than how they do it. items.title: From Benchmarks to Behaviors: A Framework for Auditing AI Agents
items.text: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate access to information. Their behavior depends on tools, instructions, and user memories that are often difficult for researchers to observe or control. Here, I introduce TRACE (Transparent Research on Agent Contexts and Environments), a framework for systematically auditing how these components shape AI agent behavior. Built on an open-source agent harness, TRACE enables controlled manipulation of system components. It also records inputs, outputs, and task execution for downstream analysis. I demonstrate this framework through an experiment examining how user memories influence source selection when agents answer questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. I find that memories expressing explicit preference for a publisher increase its inclusion among the first three cited sources in a response by 33-39 percentage points. items.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
items.text: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. items.text: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existing reasoning compression methods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. items.text: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. items.text: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. items.title: ProofPaths: An AI Agent Framework for Assessing Student Reasoning
items.text: Students can use large language models to complete assignments, but a correct solution does not establish whether they understand the reasoning behind it. Individualized interviews can probe that understanding but require recurring staff effort. We introduce ProofPaths, an AI agentic framework that combines rubric-based grading with individualized and interactive interviews. Multiple grading agents assess a submission against instructor guidance, exchange critiques, and revise their judgments. Their scores determine which review supplies the grade and feedback. An interview agent asks students to justify steps in their submission and uses their answers to guide follow-up questions. Each question is linked to a retrieved submission excerpt, so instructors can compare the student's explanation with the cited passage. The system tracks assessment progress and stores grading reviews and interview transcripts for each submission. Several deterministic tests of the assessment controllers check source handling, score aggregation, and limits on correction attempts. Instructors can inspect all reviews and transcripts and override grades within the assignment workflow.

items.text: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. items.text:
Expanded with some lessons learned (so far):


Rowan Cheung (@rowancheung)



Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:



1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter



Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.



Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).



2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation



Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.



We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.



With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)



3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem



We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.



A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 



Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.



4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive



Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.



Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 



For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.



5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

items.title: Networked AI: Architecture, Theory, and Applications
items.text: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly large-scale deep learning, have been driven by monolithic or offline training on massive curated datasets. While successful, these approaches face structural limitations: escalating data and computational demands, limited online adaptability, and a lack of system-level intelligence in open, non-stationary environments. This paper presents Networked AI - a networked intelligent system composed of interacting, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving AI agents. We establish a hierarchical layered architecture comprising an Agent Layer for heterogeneous capability construction, an Interaction Layer for signal-processing-guided online data extraction, and a Regulation Layer for stability-constrained collective evolution. Foundations in data science, signal processing, and system control are hereby synthesized into a unified theoretical framework of Networked AI, providing superior data efficiency, intelligence efficiency, interpretability, and scalability. items.text: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. items.text: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) demands reliable detection of human-authored versus synthetic text. However, current Transformer-based detectors often experience severe performance degradation during domain shifts and operate as opaque classifiers. items.title: You don't need long context
items.text: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.
